title: Erasure scope excludes backups, dead-letter, messaging layer and restore
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Previously verified fixed; delta checked for regression, none found. Round 3 at 3d33397: no regression found; the fix is still present at the cited lines (line numbers updated to 3d33397). Earlier evidence: Round 2 at d87700d. REQ-18 (l.50) extends erasure to the event store, dead-letter store, messaging layer and derived aggregates, with backups purged within 35 days. REQ-30 (l.62) adds a deletion ledger re-applied after any restore. AC-11.2 (l.165), AC-11.5 (l.168), AC-12.2 (l.175) and AC-12.4 (l.177) test each store and the restore case. Every part of the round 1 fix is present. Residual issues are raised separately as CR-024, CR-026 and CR-027.
rationale: Art. 17 erasure must reach every copy the controller holds, or the residual copies must be documented and kept out of use (for example, deletion is re-applied after a restore). As written, a subject's data survives an erasure in backups (indefinitely for DSAR), in dead-letter messages (raw, up to 7 days) and in the broker. A restore can bring erased data back.
recommended_fix: Add a REQ/AC: DSAR deletion covers primary store, dead-letter store, messaging layer and derived aggregates, and backups within a stated bound (e.g. 35 days). Keep a non-identifying deletion ledger that is re-applied after any restore. Add the restore case to AC-12.2.
verification: Re-checked by reading the PRD at 3d33397 (git show 3d33397:docs/requirements/event-analytics.md) at the cited lines.

title: Messaging layer persists raw PII without limit, contradicting REQ-16
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Previously verified fixed; delta checked for regression, none found. Round 3 at 3d33397: no regression found; the fix is still present at the cited lines (line numbers updated to 3d33397). Earlier evidence: Round 2 at d87700d. REQ-16 (l.48) declares messaging-layer persistence to be at-rest storage, bounds it to 24 h after the intake step acknowledges an event, and requires encryption under NFR-12. The messaging layer and its backups are now in the AC-13.1 (l.184) and NFR-17 (l.262) scans. AC-13.6 (l.189) tests the bound. The maximum age of unacknowledged events is routed to Q-32. Residual issues are raised as CR-032.
rationale: 'In transit' silently covers durable at-rest storage of raw email, phone, IP and user id. That is an internal contradiction and an unbounded PII store with no scan or retention control.
recommended_fix: State explicitly that broker persistence is at-rest storage. Set a maximum broker retention for raw events (e.g. no more than X hours after acknowledgement by the stripper), apply NFR-12 encryption to it, and add the broker and its backups to the AC-13.1/NFR-17 scans. Alternatively require stripping before publish in the client kit, and record that as a PO decision.
verification: Re-checked by reading the PRD at 3d33397 (git show 3d33397:docs/requirements/event-analytics.md) at the cited lines.

title: Unauthorised and revoked publishers are accepted into the dead-letter store
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Previously verified fixed; delta checked for regression, none found. Round 3 at 3d33397: no regression found; the fix is still present at the cited lines (line numbers updated to 3d33397). Earlier evidence: Round 2 at d87700d. REQ-26 (l.58) says publishes with an unknown, revoked or expired credential are refused at the messaging layer, counted, audited and never stored, including in the dead-letter store. REQ-6 (l.38) limits dead-lettering to authenticated producers, attributes it to the tenant of the credential, and bounds it per credential and per tenant. AC-9.1 (l.145), AC-15.4 (l.211) and AC-17.3, 17.4 and 17.6 (l.237-240) test this. A new flood path through the audit log is raised as CR-028.
rationale: A revoked or leaked credential can write unbounded data, including arbitrary 'PII', into platform storage. It can also fill the dead-letter store and the admin screen (DoS) and inflate another tenant's dead-letter counts. Revocation then does not actually stop the writes. This also fixes a design choice (dead-letter rather than refusal at the broker) inside the requirements.
recommended_fix: Require that publishes with an unknown, revoked or expired credential are refused at the messaging layer and only counted/audited, never stored. Keep dead-lettering for authenticated producers whose payload is invalid or which target the wrong tenant. Bound dead-letter storage per credential and per tenant, and define which tenant a cross-tenant attempt is attributed to.
verification: Re-checked by reading the PRD at 3d33397 (git show 3d33397:docs/requirements/event-analytics.md) at the cited lines.

title: Lawful basis, ePrivacy, DPIA and transparency not stated
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Previously verified fixed; delta checked for regression, none found. Round 3 at 3d33397: no regression found; the fix is still present at the cited lines (line numbers updated to 3d33397). Earlier evidence: Round 2 at d87700d. REQ-31 (l.63) and NFR-23 (l.268) state the proposed lawful basis, legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f)), plus a DPIA before HG-4, a RoPA entry, producer privacy notices and controller/processor roles. A-6 (l.278) acknowledges ePrivacy. D-5 to D-7 (l.288-290) route DPO or legal sign-off to before HG-4. The device hash is dropped. The round 1 verification criterion (items present plus a routed sign-off) is met. The new contradiction with Q-38 is raised as CR-025. The DPO sign-off itself is still outstanding.
rationale: The charter (Section 6) requires the PRD to state privacy obligations. Without consent, a lawful basis and an ePrivacy position are prerequisites, and the device-id choice may be unlawful without consent. This is not a compliance assessment; a DPO/legal review is needed.
recommended_fix: Add NFRs or dependencies: stated lawful basis per data element; ePrivacy position on device id (or drop the device hash); DPIA completed before HG-4; producer onboarding obligation to provide a privacy notice; RoPA entry. Revisit A-6.
verification: Re-checked by reading the PRD at 3d33397 (git show 3d33397:docs/requirements/event-analytics.md) at the cited lines.

title: Admin role protected by password only
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Previously verified fixed; delta checked for regression, none found. Round 3 at 3d33397: no regression found; the fix is still present at the cited lines (line numbers updated to 3d33397). Earlier evidence: Round 2 at d87700d. REQ-13 (l.45) and REQ-27 (l.59) require TOTP MFA for the admin role. AC-8.4 (l.138) blocks the admin screen without a valid TOTP code. AC-8.5 (l.139) requires a 5-minute step-up. Enrolment and lost-device reset are covered in AC-16.1, 16.5 and 16.9 (l.221, 225, 229). Remaining gaps are raised as CR-029 and CR-030.

recommended_fix: Require MFA for role admin (and optionally for all users) plus step-up re-authentication for DSAR export/deletion, dead-letter inspection and credential creation. Alternatively record an explicit PO/Security Lead risk acceptance for v1 staging-only use.

title: No-loss durability contradicts RPO 5 min
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Previously verified fixed; delta checked for regression, none found. Round 3 at 3d33397: no regression found; the fix is still present at the cited lines (line numbers updated to 3d33397). Earlier evidence: Round 2 at d87700d. AC-4.4 (l.103) tests it and C-9 (l.405) records the reconciliation.
rationale: An implementer cannot satisfy both literally. Testers will not know whether a 5-minute gap after restore is a pass.
recommended_fix: State that NFR-5 covers consumer outages and NFR-7 covers store loss, with an accepted loss window. Or require replay from the broker to close the RPO gap, and tie it to the broker retention bound.

title: Deduplication scope and window undefined
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Previously verified fixed; delta checked for regression, none found. Round 3 at 3d33397: no regression found; the fix is still present at the cited lines (line numbers updated to 3d33397). Earlier evidence: Round 2 at d87700d. REQ-7 (l.39) sets the deduplication key as (tenant, event id), with a 7-day window proposed in Q-33 (l.384). AC-15.2 (l.209), AC-15.5 to 15.7 (l.212-214) and AC-7.2 (l.129, duplicate ids across tenants) test it. The privacy side effect of keeping the ids of erased events is raised as CR-026.
rationale: With a global key, one tenant's producer can suppress another tenant's events by reusing ids (cross-tenant interference). An unbounded window has storage and cost implications. A redelivery after erasure can bring a deleted event back.
recommended_fix: Define the dedup key as (tenant, event id), set a dedup window, and add ACs for replay of an already-stored id and redelivery after deletion.

title: Retention unit inconsistent and bounds undefined
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Previously verified fixed; delta checked for regression, none found. Round 3 at 3d33397: no regression found; the fix is still present at the cited lines (line numbers updated to 3d33397). Earlier evidence: Round 2 at d87700d. AC-12.3 (l.176) rejects missing, non-numeric, fractional, zero, negative and out-of-range values and accepts 1 and 396. AC-12.5 (l.178) adds a confirmation step before a shortening that destroys data. NFR-15 (l.260) is aligned.
rationale: Without a maximum, storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)) is not enforced. Retention 0 or a negative value could trigger mass deletion.

title: Right to object excluded although the lawful basis is legitimate interests
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Previously verified fixed; delta checked for regression, none found. Round 3 at 3d33397. REQ-33 (l.65) brings Art. 21 objection into v1 as a per-tenant suppression list: new events are dropped at intake and counted, the entry persists after erasure, and changes are audited and need step-up. US-18 (AC-18.1 to AC-18.6, l.258-263) tests this, including after erasure (AC-18.2). REQ-18 (l.50) and AC-18.6 (l.263) define a manual process for rectification and restriction (owner, log, one-month deadline, DPO approval). title: Brute-force controls missing for TOTP, step-up and cross-account password attempts
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Not reworked (round 8 table l.471). AC-8.3 (l.141) changed only to add step-up for admin unlock; its clause that a lockout never applies to an already established session is unchanged, and AC-8.6 (l.144) still states no step-up context. No AC covers failed step-up attempts. Still open. Prior evidence: Round 3 at 3d33397. Partly fixed. Fixed: AC-8.6 (l.142) counts TOTP failures towards lockout (5 in 15 minutes), AC-8.7 (l.143) rejects replay, and AC-8.8 (l.144) adds per-source and global throttles. Still open: step-up. The round 2 evidence named "failed TOTP codes at sign-in or step-up". AC-8.6 is written for "5 failed TOTP codes", with no context stated. AC-8.3 (l.139) says that "a lockout never ... applies to an already established session". Step-up (AC-8.5 l.141) happens inside an established session, so a lockout caused by failed step-up codes does not stop that session from trying again. A hijacked admin session, which is the threat step-up exists for, can therefore keep guessing the step-up password and TOTP without limit. No AC tests failed step-up attempts. The new availability problem in AC-8.8 is raised separately as CR-event-analytics-036.
rationale: Without attempt limits, an attacker who has an admin password can brute-force the 6-digit TOTP code (OWASP A07).
recommended_fix: State that failed step-up attempts (password or TOTP) count towards the AC-8.6 lockout, and that reaching the limit during step-up ends the current session and is audited. This should be an explicit exception to the AC-8.3 clause about established sessions. Add an AC for 5 failed step-up codes in one session.
verification: An AC exists in which 5 failed step-up attempts in one session terminate that session and lock the account, and AC-8.3 no longer contradicts it.

title: Deletion ledger readable only by the purge process, yet intake and replay must check it
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Verified fixed. REQ-30 (l.62) and AC-11.5 (l.177) now name the same readers (intake and replay checks) and a single writer (purge process), and both state that the checks match erased (tenant, event id) values only and that the subject hash is used only for restore re-application. REQ-18 (l.50) and AC-11.2 (l.174) use the same wording. AC-11.9 (l.181) tests both required cases: a new event id for an erased, unsuppressed subject is stored; a redelivered or replayed erased event id is not. REQ-30 states that erasure is not an objection. Residual observation, not raised: the term purge process is not defined, and AC-11.2 adds messaging-layer event ids to the ledger during the admin-run erasure, so the design must treat the erasure executor as part of the purge process to keep the single-writer rule. Superseded evidence: REQ-30 (l.62) says the ledger "may be accessed only by the purge process", and AC-11.5 (l.175) says it "is readable only by the purge process". AC-11.2 (l.172) requires the subject's messaging-layer and dead-letter messages to be "excluded from intake and replay through the ledger check". AC-11.2 also deletes the subject's dedup-state entries ("event ids are retained only in the ledger"). So for an erased event, the only thing that can stop re-storage on redelivery (AC-15.7 l.226, REQ-7 l.39) is a ledger lookup by intake. Intake and replay are therefore ledger readers, which REQ-30 forbids. The scope of the check is also undefined. Matching on event ids excludes only the erased events. Matching on the keyed hash of (tenant, pseudonymous id) would drop all new events of an erased subject for 70 days, which makes erasure an undeclared objection and conflicts with AC-18.2 (l.259). That AC implies that a suppression entry is needed to stop new events.
rationale: An implementer must break either the access rule or the no-re-storage rule. One choice resurrects erased events on redelivery (an Art. 17 failure). The other silently suppresses a subject who did not object.
recommended_fix: Allow read access to the ledger for the intake and replay checks, with the purge process as the only writer. State that the check matches erased (tenant, event id) values only, and that the subject hash is used only for restore re-application. Update REQ-30, AC-11.2 and AC-11.5 to match.
verification: REQ-30, AC-11.2 and AC-11.5 name the same set of ledger readers. An AC shows a new event (new event id) for an erased subject with no suppression entry being stored, and a redelivered erased event id not being stored.

title: Erased subjects' dead-letter bodies remain revealable, and AC-11.7 contradicts the AC-10.6 reveal
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Verified fixed. REQ-15 (l.47), AC-10.6 (l.167) and AC-11.7 (l.179) now agree that unparseable bodies are never displayed or revealable and expire within 7 days, so the contradiction is gone (C-16 l.510). AC-11.2 (l.174) and REQ-18 (l.50) delete the erased subject parseable dead-letter messages immediately, and AC-11.10 (l.182) tests that a matched message cannot be found, opened or revealed after erasure. Superseded evidence: AC-11.7 (l.177) says that when an erasure is executed, unparseable dead-letter bodies "cannot be matched to a subject ... and none is displayed or replayable". AC-10.6 (l.165) and REQ-15 (l.47) say unparseable bodies can be shown through an audited reveal with a reason and step-up. AC-11.7 does not say whether the ban covers all unparseable bodies, the bodies present at erasure time, or the period until expiry. A body that cannot be matched to the erased subject cannot be singled out either, so the clause can only be implemented as a global ban, which removes the AC-10.6 reveal. Also, AC-11.2 (l.172) only excludes the erased subject's parseable dead-letter messages from intake and replay. They stay in the dead-letter store for up to 7 days, and AC-10.4 (l.163) still lets an admin open them and reveal raw PII of a subject whose erasure has been executed.
rationale: The two ACs cannot both pass. Raw PII of an erased subject stays accessible to people after erasure, which weakens the Art. 17 outcome that the round 2 fix (CR-027) accepted only as exclusion plus expiry.
recommended_fix: Make AC-11.7 an explicit rule: either unparseable bodies are never revealable (and AC-10.6 is changed to match), or reveal remains possible (and AC-11.7 drops "none is displayed"). Add to AC-11.2 that parseable dead-letter messages matched to an erased subject are deleted immediately or are no longer inspectable or revealable.
verification: AC-10.6 and AC-11.7 agree. An AC shows that after an erasure, the matched dead-letter messages of the subject cannot be opened or revealed.

title: Global sign-in throttle lets an attacker lock out all staff and contradicts the claim that a legitimate admin can still sign in
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Not reworked. AC-8.8 (l.146) is unchanged apart from whitespace (normalised comparison with 3d33397), still claims a legitimate admin from another source can still sign in, and source is still undefined. Still open. Prior evidence: AC-8.8 (l.144) says that above 200 failures in 5 minutes across all sources, "new sign-ins are limited to 10 per minute system-wide", and that "a legitimate admin from another source can still sign in". An attacker who spreads failures over 11 or more sources (each below the per-source limit of 20 in 5 minutes) triggers the global limit. The attacker then keeps using the 10 slots per minute, so legitimate users and admins compete with attack traffic and cannot reliably sign in. This is an account-independent denial of service that needs no valid credentials. The final clause of AC-8.8 cannot be guaranteed under these conditions, so it cannot be tested. "Source" is undefined. If it means the IP address, all staff behind one office NAT share one source, and one attacker or a few typos refuse the whole office for 15 minutes. Engaging a throttle is not in the REQ-20 audit list (l.52), and no metric or alert is defined for it.
rationale: Brute-force controls added for CR-029 create a cheap way to deny all dashboard and admin access, and the AC claims a property that the mechanism does not provide.
recommended_fix: Apply the global limit only to sign-in attempts that fail, or exempt sessions that have already passed the password step for a known account. Alternatively, choose a different global control such as proof-of-work or a CAPTCHA. Define "source". Audit throttle engagement and expose it as an alert-ready metric. Reword or remove the "legitimate admin can still sign in" clause so that it can be tested.
verification: In a test with 11 sources each sending 19 failures per 5 minutes, a legitimate admin signs in within a stated bound, and the throttle engagement is audited and exposed as a metric.

title: Step-up list declared exact omits MFA reset, which REQ-27 and AC-16.9 require step-up for
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Verified fixed. REQ-27 (l.59) and AC-8.5 (l.143) list the same 16 actions in the same order and both call the list a minimum the design may extend; exactly is dropped. MFA reset, entitlement grant, account unlock, allow-list changes and restriction-list changes are added, and AC-8.3 (l.141), AC-9.2 (l.153), AC-13.8 (l.205) and AC-16.9 (l.246) reference step-up consistently. R-4 (l.344) says at least 16 actions, matching the count. NFR-10 (l.296) refers to the REQ-27 actions. Superseded evidence: REQ-27 (l.59) says step-up is required "before exactly these actions", and the list has 11 items. AC-8.5 (l.141) says "the list is exactly the list in REQ-27". The same REQ-27 then says that a lost MFA device is reset "by another admin (with step-up)", and AC-16.9 (l.241) says "another admin (after step-up) resets that admin's MFA". MFA reset is not one of the 11 items. Other account-takeover actions outside the closed list have no stated position either: entitlement grants, account unlock (AC-8.3), and allow-list changes, where an added key can let new property values into storage.
rationale: An exact list is a ceiling that implementers and tests will follow. MFA reset is an account-takeover primitive: a hijacked admin session can reset another admin's MFA, and with that admin's password can enrol its own device. The PRD contradicts itself on whether this action needs step-up.
recommended_fix: Add MFA reset to the REQ-27 and AC-8.5 lists. Decide explicitly whether entitlement grant, account unlock and allow-list changes need step-up. Alternatively, drop "exactly" and state the list as a minimum.
verification: REQ-27, AC-8.5 and AC-16.9 agree on MFA reset, and R-4 (l.325) shows the updated count.

title: Objection stops new events but stored data stays in processing; Art. 17(1)(c) and compelling grounds not addressed
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Verified fixed. REQ-33 (l.65) and AC-18.1 (l.263) state that recording an objection runs the REQ-18 / AC-11.2 erasure for the same pairs in the same flow; the old clause that stored data is not changed is removed. AC-18.7 (l.269) records the per-store outcome, keeps the suppression on failure and allows a step-up re-run. This review is not legal advice; D-5 sign-off still applies. Superseded evidence: AC-18.1 (l.258) says "earlier stored data is not changed by the objection", and REQ-33 (l.65) acts only on new events. Under Art. 21(1), on objection to processing based on Art. 6(1)(f), the controller "shall no longer process the personal data" unless it demonstrates compelling legitimate grounds. Art. 17(1)(c) then gives a right to erasure. As written, an objecting subject's stored events keep being processed and keep counting in unique users for up to 396 days. No requirement says that an objection triggers erasure, prompts the admin to run one, or records compelling grounds. D-5 (l.313) does not ask the DPO to decide this.
rationale: The round 2 fix brought objection into v1 only for future collection. Continued processing of stored data after an objection is a likely compliance gap, and the PRD contains no decision on it. A legal position is needed, and this review is not legal advice.
recommended_fix: Either state that an objection also runs the AC-11.2 erasure for the same pairs (or offers it as a step in the same flow, and records the outcome), or record DPO-approved compelling grounds for keeping the data. Add this question to D-5.
verification: REQ-33 states what happens to stored data on objection. There is an AC for it, or D-5 lists the DPO decision.

title: Manual rectification and restriction rely on direct operator store changes with no mechanism, audit or restriction semantics
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Verified fixed against the round 3 verification criteria. Restriction is a product mechanism (REQ-34 l.66, US-19 AC-19.1 to AC-19.7 l.275-281). Rectification is stated as not applicable pending DPO confirmation (REQ-18 l.50, AC-18.6 l.268, D-5 l.332). Manual data changes run as audited, reviewed scripts (AC-14.7 l.219) and runs of manual data-change scripts are in the REQ-20 list (l.52). Residual gaps in the new restriction mechanism are raised as CR-event-analytics-048 and in AC-14.7 as CR-event-analytics-051. Superseded evidence: REQ-18 (l.50) and AC-18.6 (l.263) say that rectification and restriction are applied manually by "an operator with deployment-level access", with only the outcome recorded in a separate log. Restriction (Art. 18) means keeping the data but no longer processing it. The platform has no flag or mechanism that excludes a subject's stored events from aggregates while keeping them, so an operator would have to edit or move records directly in the event store. The REQ-20 audit list (l.52) and AC-14.4 (l.212), which covers deployment configuration only, do not cover direct data-store changes. Such edits would also break the aggregate-recount invariant of AC-11.2 and the restore and ledger logic. Nothing says how a restricted subject is kept out of re-processing (REQ-16) or out of a restore.
rationale: The process cannot be carried out without unaudited privileged data changes, which is a security and integrity gap on a Tier 3 system. Restriction has no defined outcome that anyone could verify.
recommended_fix: Define restriction as a per-tenant restriction-list entry, similar to REQ-33, that excludes the subject's stored events from queries while keeping them. Alternatively, state that restriction is implemented by suppression plus an export to cold storage. Require any manual data change to run as an audited, reviewed script whose run is in REQ-20. Rectification of pseudonymous analytics events may reasonably be "not applicable"; if so, ask the DPO to confirm that under D-5.
verification: REQ-18 and AC-18.6 name the mechanism for each right, and REQ-20 covers the manual change.

title: Restore can lose recent deletion-ledger and suppression-list entries within the 5-minute RPO, so erased data can reappear
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Verified fixed against the round 3 verification criterion. NFR-26 (l.312) sets RPO 0, synchronous durability and separate backup for the ledger, suppression list, restriction list and audit log; NFR-7 (l.293) and AC-4.4 (l.105) now scope the 5-minute loss window to the event store only; AC-4.6 (l.107) tests an erasure, a suppression entry, a restriction entry and their audit records created 1 minute before an event-store failure, and AC-19.7 (l.281) covers restriction after restore. C-9 and C-19 (l.503, l.513) are consistent. Residual test gap raised as CR-event-analytics-049. Superseded evidence: NFR-7 (l.275) and AC-4.4 (l.104) accept up to 5 minutes of data loss on restore. REQ-30 (l.62) and REQ-33 (l.65) add a ledger and a suppression list, and AC-12.4 (l.187) and AC-18.2 (l.259) require both to survive a restore. No requirement states the RPO for the ledger, the suppression list or the audit log, or says that they are stored separately from the event store. If the ledger is restored from the same backup as the event store, an erasure executed in the last 5 minutes before the failure is lost from the ledger, and the restored subject data is served again. A suppression entry added in that window is also lost silently, and the objection stops having effect.
rationale: Re-applying the ledger after a restore is only safe if the ledger is more durable than the data it acts on. Otherwise erased data comes back without any error being raised.
recommended_fix: State RPO 0 (or synchronous, separately backed-up durability) for the ledger, suppression list and audit log. Alternatively, require that after a restore, any erasure or objection executed within the RPO window is re-run from the audit trail before queries are served.
verification: An AC exists: an erasure and a suppression added 1 minute before a store failure are both effective after the restore.

title: Pending HG-C charter amendment understates raw-PII retention in the messaging layer relative to PRD revision 9
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Verified fixed on the HG-C branch, not on main. git show origin/docs/hg-c-charter-pii:docs/project-charter.md (head 7465f52, commit message cites CR-041) l.64-68: raw PII is not persisted beyond the bounds below, and is held in the messaging layer at most 24 h after intake acknowledgement or 7 days if never acknowledged, and in dead-letter messages up to 7 days. REQ-16 (l.48) and R-2 (l.342) are unchanged at cf5c048 apart from whitespace, so the texts match. 7465f52 is not an ancestor of origin/main; HG-C (PR #4) is still awaiting. Superseded evidence: git show 1afb371:docs/project-charter.md l.62-68 says that raw PII is "never persisted" and is held "in the messaging layer (at most 24 h after stripping)". PRD revision 9 (REQ-16 l.48, AC-13.6 l.199, R-2 l.323, confirmed Q-32 l.402) allows up to 7 days for unacknowledged events, and up to 24 hours after acknowledgement rather than after stripping. It also states that messaging-layer persistence is at-rest storage. The PRD says it "depends on that amendment" (l.9). This is the pending amendment, not the main-branch charter, which is out of scope per instructions.
rationale: If HG-C approves the charter as written, the HG-0 artifact will describe a smaller PII exposure than the approved requirements and the DPIA input. That misstates risk in the governing document.
recommended_fix: Update the amendment to "at most 24 h after intake acknowledgement and 7 days if never acknowledged, plus dead-letter messages up to 7 days", and replace "never persisted" with "not persisted beyond these bounds".
verification: The amendment text matches REQ-16 and R-2 before HG-C is decided.

title: Future-timestamp bound is relative to the producer-controlled send time, so future-dated events are unbounded
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Not reworked. REQ-28 (l.60) and AC-15.3 (l.227) are unchanged apart from whitespace. Still open. Prior evidence: REQ-28 (l.60) and AC-15.3 (l.222) dead-letter an event whose event time is more than 24 h after the client kit's send time. The send time is set by the producer host, normally from the same clock as the event time, and nothing checks it against ingest time. A host whose clock is a year ahead, or a publisher that sets both fields, gets far-future events accepted. They then appear in future UTC days and distort previous-period comparisons. The past bound is measured against ingest time, so the two bounds use different reference clocks. Round 2 suggested send time to avoid false rejections, and that part works. This finding is about the missing upper bound against a trusted clock.
rationale: This is a data-quality hole that one misconfigured producer can cause. Retention is not affected, because it uses ingest time.
recommended_fix: Also dead-letter events whose send time is more than a stated bound (for example 24 h) after ingest time. Keep the event-time-vs-send-time rule for device skew.
verification: An AC for send time = ingest + 2 days results in dead-letter with reason "timestamp_out_of_bounds".

title: Re-processing capability that justifies 24 h post-acknowledgement raw-PII retention is not specified, audited or tested
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Not reworked. REQ-20 (l.52) was extended for restriction and manual scripts but still does not list re-processing of raw events, and no REQ or AC defines the re-processing capability. Still open. Prior evidence: Q-47 (l.440) and REQ-16 (l.48) justify keeping raw events 24 h after acknowledgement for "re-processing after a failure detected after acknowledgement". No requirement or AC defines this capability: who triggers it, through which interface, how it interacts with dedup (REQ-7 l.39: re-processed events that are already in the dedup state would be skipped, which defeats recovery after a store loss), and with the ledger and suppression checks. Re-processing raw PII is also not in the REQ-20 audit list (l.52).
rationale: Under the storage-limitation principle, the purpose has to be real and exercised. Here it is stated but not specified, so the 24 h of raw PII has no testable justification, and an unaudited raw-PII replay path is left to design.
recommended_fix: Add a requirement and an AC for operator-triggered re-processing: audited, subject to the ledger and suppression checks, and with defined dedup behaviour. Alternatively, reduce the post-acknowledgement retention.
verification: A REQ and an AC exist for re-processing, and REQ-20 lists it.

title: AC-14.6 bound of 10 per-minute records in 10 minutes is off by one for windows not aligned to the minute
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Not reworked. AC-14.6 (l.218) and NFR-25 (l.311) still say at most 10 platform-level records in 10 minutes. Still open. Prior evidence: AC-14.6 (l.214) and NFR-25 (l.293) say that 1,000,000 refusals within 10 minutes produce "at most 10 platform-level refusal audit records (one per minute with a count)". A 10-minute test that does not start exactly on a minute boundary touches 11 calendar-minute buckets, so a correct per-minute aggregator produces 11 records and fails the AC.
rationale: The AC is flaky or fails for a correct implementation.
recommended_fix: Use "at most 11", or define the buckets relative to the test window.
verification: AC-14.6 and NFR-25 are reworded.

title: Verification-reference tenant coverage is self-attested by the admin running the request
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Not reworked. AC-11.1 (l.173), R-15 (l.355) and D-8 (l.335) are unchanged apart from whitespace; the new AC-19.6 (l.280) repeats the same self-attested coverage check for restriction. Still open. Prior evidence: AC-11.1 (l.171) and AC-18.5 (l.262) refuse a pair whose tenant "is not covered by the verification reference". The verification process is outside the system (D-8 l.316), so the system can only compare the pairs with a tenant list that the same admin types in. The check then catches typing errors but not a wrong or misused reference. R-15 (l.336) cites this check as its mitigation, and with one person holding all roles (R-5 l.326) there is no second check.
rationale: The control reads as a system guarantee, but it is a single-person attestation.
recommended_fix: State that the reference and its tenant list are entered by the admin and are evidence only, and give R-15 a compensating control (for example, the verification log is checked against DSAR runs at HG-4 or periodically). Alternatively, require a second person to enter the reference.
verification: AC-11.1 and R-15 state the actual strength of the check.

title: Dead-letter bounds count messages, not bytes
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Not reworked. REQ-6 (l.38), AC-15.4 (l.228) and AC-15.8 (l.232) are unchanged apart from whitespace; no byte bound. Still open. Prior evidence: REQ-6 (l.38) and AC-15.4 (l.223) bound the dead-letter store at 10,000 messages per credential and 100,000 per tenant. Oversize messages (above 64 KB) are dead-lettered (AC-15.8 l.227). No byte bound or maximum stored body size is stated. With 10 or more tenants (NFR-8), the store can grow to 100,000 messages per tenant times the broker's maximum message size, and each of those bodies holds raw PII for 7 days.
rationale: A storage-exhaustion risk from one authenticated producer, which also increases the volume of raw PII held.
recommended_fix: Truncate the stored body of oversize messages (for example to 64 KB plus a hash) or set a byte bound per credential and per tenant.
verification: REQ-6 or AC-15.8 states a byte bound.

title: Gate state binds HG-1 to PRD revision 5 (59d8755) while revision 9 is under review
evidence: Round 4 at cf5c048. Verified fixed for the stated issue. git show cf5c048:.sdlc/state/event-analytics.json: gates.HG-1.sha is 3d33397 and artifacts.prd is revision 9 at 3d33397, set in review commit 3933df7, so HG-1 is no longer bound to revision 5. cf5c048 did not touch the state file, which is consistent with keeping gate edits out of PRD commits; the orchestrator must re-bind HG-1 and artifacts.prd to revision 11 (cf5c048) in the round 4 review commit. Superseded evidence: git show 3d33397:.sdlc/state/event-analytics.json records artifacts.prd as revision 5 at sha 59d8755, HG-1 as "awaiting" with sha 59d8755, and head_sha e1d18fe. The PRD under review is revision 9 at 3d33397 (header l.3).
rationale: An HG-1 approval recorded against this state would bind to a superseded revision.
recommended_fix: The orchestrator updates artifacts.prd and gates.HG-1.sha to the SHA that is actually submitted for HG-1, in a non-PRD commit.
verification: The state file shows the PRD revision and SHA that the PO approves.

title: Restriction list has no erasure, retention-purge or subject-access semantics
evidence: New in revision 11. REQ-34 (l.66) and AC-19.1 (l.275) exclude a restricted subject stored events from every query while keeping them, and entries are removed only with a verification reference (AC-19.5 l.279). Three interactions are undefined. (1) Erasure: the REQ-18 erasure scope (l.50) and AC-11.2 (l.174) do not include the restriction list, and unlike the suppression list (REQ-33 l.65) no reason is given for keeping it; after an erasure or an objection-triggered erasure (AC-18.1 l.263) the (tenant, pseudonymous id) entry remains indefinitely with no purpose and no retention bound, outside the 70-day ledger limit (REQ-30 l.62). (2) Retention purge: AC-12.1 (l.188) purges by ingest time with no exception, so restricted data is destroyed at retention expiry, although Art. 18(1)(b) and (c) restriction exists to keep data the subject needs (for example for legal claims); the PRD neither keeps it nor states that purge proceeds. (3) Subject access: AC-19.1 says every query excludes the subject events; it is not stated whether a DSAR access export (AC-11.1 l.173) for a restricted subject still returns them, which Art. 15 requires.
rationale: The new mechanism is complete for queries only. Implementers will choose silently between keeping pseudonymous ids of erased subjects forever and deleting them, between destroying restricted data at retention and holding it past retention, and between returning or hiding it in an access export. Each choice has a GDPR consequence that the PO and DPO should decide. This is not legal advice.
recommended_fix: State that erasure (including objection-triggered erasure) also removes the subject restriction-list entry, or give a purpose and retention bound for keeping it. State whether retention purge applies to restricted data (and add the question to D-5 if a hold is wanted). State that subject access exports include restricted events. Add one AC per rule.
verification: REQ-18 or REQ-34 states the restriction-list outcome on erasure; REQ-34 or REQ-17 states the retention-purge rule for restricted data; AC-11.1 or AC-19.x states that an access export includes restricted events; each has an AC.

title: RPO 0 for privacy-control stores is tested only against event-store failure, and the 5-second audit write window contradicts RPO 0 for the audit log
evidence: New in revision 11. NFR-26 (l.312) requires RPO 0 with synchronous durability for the ledger, suppression list, restriction list and audit log. AC-4.6 (l.107) and AC-19.7 (l.281) test only an event-store failure, in which those separately stored lists are not affected, so the tests pass without exercising the RPO 0 property. No AC covers failure and restore of the store holding those lists, or a joint failure of both stores (for example one host or volume in the Docker environments, REQ-22), which is the case where a lost ledger entry lets erased data return. AC-14.1 (l.213) allows an audit record to be written up to 5 seconds after the action, so an action acknowledged to the admin can have an audit record that is not yet durable, which is not RPO 0. AC-4.6 uses records created 1 minute before the failure, outside that window.
rationale: The test set can pass while the property NFR-26 claims is not met; the residual risk is reappearance of erased data after a joint restore.
recommended_fix: Add an AC that fails and restores the privacy-control store (and one joint-failure case) and checks 0 lost entries for entries created seconds before the failure. Either require the audit record to be durable before the action is reported as complete, or state that the audit RPO is the 5-second write window.
verification: ACs exist for own-store and joint failure; AC-14.1 and NFR-26 state consistent audit durability.

title: Step-up minimum omits account disable, credential revocation and dead-letter replay or discard
evidence: New observation on the reworked list. REQ-27 (l.59) and AC-8.5 (l.143) now list 16 step-up actions as a minimum. Account disable (AC-16.2 l.239), producer-credential revocation (AC-17.4 l.255) and dead-letter replay and discard (AC-10.2 l.163) are not on it. AC-16.6 (l.243) only prevents disabling the last active admin, so a hijacked admin session past the 5-minute step-up window can disable every other admin and remain the only admin, which has the same effect as the listed role change. Revocation and discard are irreversible data-affecting actions (discard deletes dead-letter data; replay stores raw-derived data).
rationale: The list is now a minimum, so the design may add these, but tests follow the listed minimum. Account disable of other admins is an account-takeover lockout primitive comparable to items already listed.
recommended_fix: Add account disable (at least for admin accounts) to REQ-27 and AC-8.5, and decide explicitly on credential revocation and dead-letter replay or discard; update R-4.
verification: REQ-27 and AC-8.5 list account disable, or record a PO decision not to; R-4 count matches.

title: Reviewed-script control for manual data changes is self-review under R-5 and its no-direct-edit clause is not testable
evidence: New in revision 11. AC-14.7 (l.219) requires that any manual change to stored data runs only as a script reviewed before the run, audited with reviewer and operator, and that no direct unscripted edit of a store is permitted. R-5 (l.345) states that a single human holds all roles, so reviewer and operator are the same person. Operators with deployment-level access (break-glass, AC-16.7 l.244) can edit stores directly, and the product cannot detect or prevent that, so the final clause is a policy statement, not a testable acceptance criterion. No compensating control is named.
rationale: The control reads as a system guarantee but is a single-person procedure, the same pattern as CR-event-analytics-045.
recommended_fix: State that AC-14.7 is a procedural control, name the compensating control under R-5 (for example an agent or second-person review recorded in the PR, plus periodic reconciliation of store row counts against the audit log), and rephrase the no-direct-edit clause as a documented prohibition with a detection measure.
verification: AC-14.7 states its control type and a compensating control is recorded in R-5 or the role register.
